title: Greedy: Non-overlapping Intervals
oneLiner: To remove as few intervals as possible, keep as many as possible: sort by END time and always keep the interval that finishes earliest.
keyTakeaway: Minimizing removals is the same as maximizing the intervals you keep. Sort by end time; walk them in order, keeping an interval whenever it starts at or after the end of the last one you kept, and counting it as removed otherwise. Finishing earliest always leaves the most room for everything after, so this greedy choice is never worse than any other: O(n log n).
explanation:
Given a list of intervals, return the minimum number you have to remove so that the rest don't overlap. Intervals that only touch, like [1, 2] and [2, 3], don't overlap. For [[1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 4], [1, 3]] the answer is 1: remove [1, 3] and the other three line up end to end.

Flip the question around: removing the fewest is the same as keeping the most, so find the largest set of intervals with no overlaps and subtract its size from n. Trying every subset is exponential. A greedy rule works instead: of all the intervals you could keep next, keep the one that ENDS earliest. Why is that safe? Suppose some best answer keeps a different interval first. Swap it for the earliest-ending one: that one ends no later, so everything after it in the best answer still fits, and the count is unchanged. Repeat the argument at every step and the greedy choice is never worse.

In code: sort the intervals by end. Track lastEnd, the end of the last interval you kept (start with nothing kept). For each interval in order: if its start >= lastEnd, it fits after what you kept, so keep it and set lastEnd to its end. Otherwise it overlaps the last kept interval, and since that one ends no later (the list is sorted by end), dropping the current one is the right call: count one removal. Sorting dominates, O(n log n) time; the pass itself is O(n) and needs only two variables.

Sorting by START is the tempting mistake. With [[1, 10], [2, 3], [4, 5], [6, 7]], sorting by start and keeping whatever comes first would keep [1, 10] and remove the other three, but the best answer removes only [1, 10]. A long interval that starts early blocks everything; ending early is what matters. The same rule (sort by end, keep the earliest finisher) answers activity selection, "maximum number of meetings in one room" and "minimum arrows to burst balloons".

The visualization shows the intervals sorted by end; the message says which ones are kept.

[2,3] ends earliest of all: keep it. lastEnd = 3. Kept so far: [[2,3]].
[1,4] starts at 1, before lastEnd = 3: it overlaps the kept interval, which ends sooner. Remove it. Kept so far: [[2,3]].
[4,5] starts at 4, at or after lastEnd = 3: it fits, keep it. lastEnd = 5. Kept so far: [[2,3], [4,5]].
[3,7] starts at 3, before lastEnd = 5: it overlaps the kept interval, which ends sooner. Remove it. Kept so far: [[2,3], [4,5]].
[6,8] starts at 6, at or after lastEnd = 5: it fits, keep it. lastEnd = 8. Kept so far: [[2,3], [4,5], [6,8]].
[1,10] starts at 1, before lastEnd = 8: it overlaps the kept interval, which ends sooner. Remove it. Kept so far: [[2,3], [4,5], [6,8]].
Done: kept [[2,3], [4,5], [6,8]], removed 3. Sorting by start instead would have kept [1,10] first and blocked almost everything.

recognitionSignals: "Remove the fewest intervals so the rest don't overlap", or the mirror image, "keep / schedule / attend the MOST non-overlapping intervals".
Picking a subset of intervals where one locally best choice (the earliest finish) can be argued never to hurt later choices.
Brute force would try subsets, but intervals give an ordering that a single sorted pass can exploit.
gotchas: Sort by END, not by start. Sorting by start and keeping the first interval of each overlapping pair keeps long intervals that block many short ones.
Touching endpoints don't overlap here, so the keep test is start >= lastEnd; using > removes intervals that could stay.
When an interval overlaps, don't update lastEnd: the interval you already kept ends no later, so it stays the one to compare against.
confusableWith: Merge Intervals (this track) also sorts intervals and walks them once, but it COMBINES overlapping intervals into one (sorted by start). Here overlapping intervals are thrown away, and the right sort key is the end.
Minimum Meeting Rooms (this track) keeps every interval and asks how many rooms they need; this one keeps a single "room" and asks how many intervals must go.

complexity.note: Sorting by end time dominates; the greedy pass is O(n) with two variables. Space is the sorted copy, or O(1) extra if you sort in place and ignore the sort's own stack.
